Chapter 20 — Hyperbola

Kanna, an ellipse keeps a sum fixed. A hyperbola keeps the size of a difference fixed. This change creates two open branches.

Your overall target remains 200 marks: Physics 60, Maths 60, Chemistry 80. Begin with orientation, foci, eccentricity and asymptotes. Then use the same geometry for tangents, distances and loci.

Concept C01 — A fixed difference gives two branches

Fix foci F1=(c,0),F2=(−c,0)F_1=(c,0),F_2=(-c,0)F1​=(c,0),F2​=(−c,0). A point PPP is on the hyperbola when

∣PF1−PF2∣=2a,0<a<c.\boxed{|PF_1-PF_2|=2a},\qquad 0<a<c.∣PF1​−PF2​∣=2a​,0<a<c.

The modulus means the positive size of the difference. One distance is larger, but the difference can have either sign before taking modulus. That is why the full locus includes both branches.

The centre is the midpoint of the foci. The nearest curve points to the centre are the vertices (±a,0)(\pm a,0)(±a,0). The line segment joining them is the transverse axis, length 2a2a2a.

For a hyperbola we use

c2=a2+b2,x2a2−y2b2=1,a,b>0.\boxed{c^2=a^2+b^2},\qquad \boxed{\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1}, \quad a,b>0.c2=a2+b2​,a2x2​−b2y2​=1​,a,b>0.

Here bbb is a second shape length. Unlike an ellipse, we do not require a>ba>ba>b. The segment joining (0,±b)(0,\pm b)(0,±b) is the conjugate axis, length 2b2b2b; those endpoints do not lie on this hyperbola.

Compare the signs: ellipse: c2=a2−b2c^2=a^2-b^2c2=a2−b2 and a plus in its equation. Hyperbola: c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2 and a minus in its equation. The foci are beyond the vertices, because c>ac>ac>a.

Concept C03 — Eccentricity, foci and directrices

e=ca=1+b2a2>1.\boxed{e=\frac ca=\sqrt{1+\frac{b^2}{a^2}}>1}.e=ac​=1+a2b2​​>1​.

The focus is farther from the centre than the corresponding vertex. The corresponding focus–directrix rule is again

PF=e PD,\boxed{PF=e\,PD},PF=ePD​,

where PDPDPD is the perpendicular distance to the directrix. For the right/left foci (±c,0)(\pm c,0)(±c,0), the matching directrices are

x=±ae=±a2c.\boxed{x=\pm\frac ae=\pm\frac{a^2}{c}}.x=±ea​=±ca2​​.

They lie between the centre and the vertices, because a/e<aa/e<aa/e<a. For a vertical hyperbola they are y=±a/ey=\pm a/ey=±a/e. Shift each with the centre when needed.

The focal separation is 2c=2ae2c=2ae2c=2ae. The directrix separation is 2a/e2a/e2a/e. These are different.

Use the clue carefully: foci (±5,0)(\pm5,0)(±5,0) give c=5c=5c=5, while vertices (±3,0)(\pm3,0)(±3,0) give a=3a=3a=3. After finding a,ca,ca,c, use b2=c2−a2b^2=c^2-a^2b2=c2−a2, not an ellipse's subtraction order.

Concept C04 — Focal distances and latus rectum

For a point on the right branch, x≥ax\ge ax≥a:

PFright=ex−a,PFleft=ex+a.\boxed{PF_{\rm right}=ex-a},\qquad \boxed{PF_{\rm left}=ex+a}.PFright​=ex−a​,PFleft​=ex+a​.

Their difference is 2a2a2a, as required. On the left branch the roles reverse. For both branches, safe absolute-value forms are

PFright=∣ex−a∣,PFleft=∣ex+a∣.\boxed{PF_{\rm right}=|ex-a|},\qquad \boxed{PF_{\rm left}=|ex+a|}.PFright​=∣ex−a∣​,PFleft​=∣ex+a∣​.

For example, the right directrix is x=a/ex=a/ex=a/e. On the right branch its distance is x−a/ex-a/ex−a/e, so multiplying by eee gives ex−aex-aex−a. The focal-distance formula comes from the actual distance rule.

The latus rectum is a chord through a focus, perpendicular to the transverse axis. Put x=cx=cx=c in the horizontal equation:

c2a2−y2b2=1⟹y=±b2a.\frac{c^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=\pm\frac{b^2}{a}.a2c2​−b2y2​=1⟹y=±ab2​.

Hence

endpoints=(c,±b2a),L=2b2a.\boxed{\text{endpoints}=\left(c,\pm\frac{b^2}{a}\right)},\qquad \boxed{L=\frac{2b^2}{a}}.endpoints=(c,±ab2​)​,L=a2b2​​.

The form of this length matches the ellipse formula, but the relation among a,b,ca,b,ca,b,c is different. The full length is twice b2/ab^2/ab2/a.

Concept C05 — An asymptote is a line the branch approaches

Far from the centre, the terms x2/a2x^2/a^2x2/a2 and y2/b2y^2/b^2y2/b2 are large. Their difference remains 1. The nearby straight-line directions come from dropping only that constant in the equation:

x2a2−y2b2=0⟹y=±bax.\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{y=\pm\frac ba x}.a2x2​−b2y2​=0⟹y=±ab​x​.

These lines are the asymptotes. The perpendicular distance of the branch from one of them tends to zero as the point moves far along that branch.

For a horizontal shifted hyperbola:

y−k=±ba(x−h).\boxed{y-k=\pm\frac ba(x-h)}.y−k=±ab​(x−h)​.

For a vertical one, use y−k=±(a/b)(x−h)y-k=\pm(a/b)(x-h)y−k=±(a/b)(x−h). Both asymptotes pass through the centre, not through a focus.

Why they are approached: for the upper right branch,

y=bax2−a2,y=\frac ba\sqrt{x^2-a^2},y=ab​x2−a2​,

so its vertical gap from y=(b/a)xy=(b/a)xy=(b/a)x is

ba(x−x2−a2)=abx+x2−a2⟶0.\frac ba\left(x-\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\right) =\frac{ab}{x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}\longrightarrow0.ab​(x−x2−a2​)=x+x2−a2​ab​⟶0.

The actual asymptote never meets this hyperbola at a finite point: substituting its equation would give 0=10=10=1. It is not a tangent touching somewhere very far away.

Angle cue: if one asymptote makes angle α=tan⁡−1(b/a)\alpha=\tan^{-1}(b/a)α=tan−1(b/a) with +x+x+x, the two sectors have angles 2α2\alpha2α and 180∘−2α180^\circ-2\alpha180∘−2α. The smaller is the acute angle when they are not perpendicular.

tan⁡θacute=∣2aba2−b2∣(a≠b).\tan\theta_{\rm acute}=\left|\frac{2ab}{a^2-b^2}\right|\quad(a\ne b).tanθacute​=​a2−b22ab​​(a=b).

If a=ba=ba=b, the asymptotes are perpendicular and the smaller angle is 90∘90^\circ90∘. Draw which angle is being asked before choosing its supplement.

Concept C06 — Conjugate and rectangular hyperbolas

The conjugate hyperbola of

x2a2−y2b2=1\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1a2x2​−b2y2​=1

is

y2b2−x2a2=1.\boxed{\frac{y^2}{b^2}-\frac{x^2}{a^2}=1}.b2y2​−a2x2​=1​.

The transverse length becomes bbb, and the other length becomes aaa. Its focal distance is still a2+b2\sqrt{a^2+b^2}a2+b2​, but its foci are vertical. The two hyperbolas have the same asymptote pair.

If their eccentricities are e,e′e,e'e,e′, then

e=a2+b2a,e′=a2+b2b,1e2+1e′2=1.e=\frac{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}a,\qquad e'=\frac{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}b,\qquad \boxed{\frac1{e^2}+\frac1{e'^2}=1}.e=aa2+b2​​,e′=ba2+b2​​,e21​+e′21​=1​.

A rectangular hyperbola has perpendicular asymptotes. In this axis-aligned form that means a=ba=ba=b, so

e=2.\boxed{e=\sqrt2}.e=2​​.

“Rectangular” describes the right angle between asymptotes. It does not mean the curve is a rectangle.

Concept C07 — Why the transverse axis of xy=Kxy=Kxy=K is sloping

For K≠0K\ne0K=0, the coordinate axes are asymptotes of xy=Kxy=Kxy=K, so they are perpendicular. It is a rectangular hyperbola.

For K>0K>0K>0, its branches are in quadrants I and III. Use actual perpendicular diagonal directions:

u=x+y2,v=x−y2.u=\frac{x+y}{\sqrt2},\qquad v=\frac{x-y}{\sqrt2}.u=2​x+y​,v=2​x−y​.

Both directions have unit length. Since xy=(u2−v2)/2xy=(u^2-v^2)/2xy=(u2−v2)/2,

xy=K⟹u22K−v22K=1.xy=K \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{u^2}{2K}-\frac{v^2}{2K}=1.xy=K⟹2Ku2​−2Kv2​=1.

Thus the transverse semiaxis is 2K\sqrt{2K}2K​ and

transverse-axis length=22K.\boxed{\text{transverse-axis length}=2\sqrt{2K}}.transverse-axis length=22K​​.

Its original-coordinate vertices are (±K,±K)(\pm\sqrt K,\pm\sqrt K)(±K​,±K​) with matching signs. If K<0K<0K<0, the branches are in II and IV, and the length is 22∣K∣2\sqrt{2|K|}22∣K∣​. At K=0K=0K=0, the equation describes two axes, not a nondegenerate hyperbola.

A convenient parameter for xy=Kxy=Kxy=K is (t,K/t)(t,K/t)(t,K/t), t≠0t\ne0t=0. Its tangent at (x1,y1)(x_1,y_1)(x1​,y1​) is

xy1+yx1=2K.\boxed{xy_1+yx_1=2K}.xy1​+yx1​=2K​.

Concept C08 — Tangents and normals at finite points

For x2/a2−y2/b2=1x^2/a^2-y^2/b^2=1x2/a2−y2/b2=1, the tangent at a verified curve point (x1,y1)(x_1,y_1)(x1​,y1​) is

xx1a2−yy1b2=1.\boxed{\frac{xx_1}{a^2}-\frac{yy_1}{b^2}=1}.a2xx1​​−b2yy1​​=1​.

The minus sign belongs to the hyperbola. Differentiation gives y′=b2x/(a2y)y'=b^2x/(a^2y)y′=b2x/(a2y) when y≠0y\ne0y=0, and the tangent formula follows from point-slope form.

A normal is perpendicular to that tangent. Its direction is (x1/a2,−y1/b2)(x_1/a^2,-y_1/b^2)(x1​/a2,−y1​/b2). When x1y1≠0x_1y_1\ne0x1​y1​=0, its equation is

a2xx1+b2yy1=a2+b2.\boxed{\frac{a^2x}{x_1}+\frac{b^2y}{y_1}=a^2+b^2}.x1​a2x​+y1​b2y​=a2+b2​.

At vertices (±a,0)(\pm a,0)(±a,0), the tangents are vertical and the normals are the horizontal axis. Handle these directly instead of dividing by zero.

For a finite-slope line y=mx+c0y=mx+c_0y=mx+c0​,

c02=a2m2−b2>0\boxed{c_0^2=a^2m^2-b^2>0}c02​=a2m2−b2>0​

is the finite-contact tangency condition. The strict inequality matters. If the right side is zero, then c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 and m=±b/am=\pm b/am=±b/a: the line is an asymptote, with no finite contact.

For a general proper line Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0, the equivalent test is

C2=a2A2−b2B2>0.\boxed{C^2=a^2A^2-b^2B^2>0}.C2=a2A2−b2B2>0​.

This also includes the vertical vertex tangents. Substitution and a repeated-root discriminant give this equation; the strict positive condition removes the asymptote degeneration.

Important for JEE Main: a zero algebraic discriminant is not enough if the intersection polynomial loses its quadratic term. Check that the proposed line actually has a finite contact point.

Concept C09 — A parameter makes a moving point satisfy the curve

The identity sec⁡2θ−tan⁡2θ=1\sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta=1sec2θ−tan2θ=1 suggests

P=(asec⁡θ,btan⁡θ),cos⁡θ≠0.\boxed{P=(a\sec\theta,b\tan\theta)},\qquad\cos\theta\ne0.P=(asecθ,btanθ)​,cosθ=0.

Substitution verifies the equation. Positive sec⁡θ\sec\thetasecθ gives the right branch and negative sec⁡θ\sec\thetasecθ the left branch.

This θ\thetaθ is a parameter, not generally the angle of OPOPOP. In fact,

yx=basin⁡θ.\frac yx=\frac ba\sin\theta.xy​=ab​sinθ.

Use the coordinates from the stated parameter before measuring a distance or an angle.

The parameter tangent is

xsec⁡θa−ytan⁡θb=1.\boxed{\frac{x\sec\theta}{a}-\frac{y\tan\theta}{b}=1}.axsecθ​−bytanθ​=1​.

It includes vertices when tan⁡θ=0\tan\theta=0tanθ=0. A shifted curve needs its centre coordinates added.

Concept C10 — A midpoint chord needs real endpoint checks

For midpoint M=(h,k)M=(h,k)M=(h,k), set endpoints (h+u,k+v),(h−u,k−v)(h+u,k+v),(h-u,k-v)(h+u,k+v),(h−u,k−v) and subtract their hyperbola equations:

hua2−kvb2=0.\frac{hu}{a^2}-\frac{kv}{b^2}=0.a2hu​−b2kv​=0.

The chord line is therefore

hxa2−kyb2=h2a2−k2b2.\boxed{\frac{hx}{a^2}-\frac{ky}{b^2} =\frac{h^2}{a^2}-\frac{k^2}{b^2}}.a2hx​−b2ky​=a2h2​−b2k2​​.

A midpoint is not necessarily on the curve. Do not replace the right side by 1 without checking.

For a proposed noncentral midpoint, verify that this line really meets the hyperbola at two distinct real points. A necessary line equation alone does not prove a real chord exists. For the centre, it becomes 0=00=00=0 and does not select a unique chord. Some lines through the centre do not meet the hyperbola at all.

Contact chord connection: if real tangents from an external point (h,k)(h,k)(h,k) touch at two finite points, their contact chord is hx/a2−ky/b2=1hx/a^2-ky/b^2=1hx/a2−ky/b2=1. This uses the external point's role, not its role as a midpoint. Asymptote candidates must not be counted as finite contacts.

Concept C11 — Two different products of perpendicular distances

From the foci to a tangent: the product is

d1d2=b2.\boxed{d_1d_2=b^2}.d1​d2​=b2​.

To see it, write a genuine tangent as Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0. Its distances from (±c,0)(\pm c,0)(±c,0) multiply to

∣C+cA∣ ∣C−cA∣A2+B2=∣C2−c2A2∣A2+B2.\frac{|C+cA|\,|C-cA|}{A^2+B^2} =\frac{|C^2-c^2A^2|}{A^2+B^2}.A2+B2∣C+cA∣∣C−cA∣​=A2+B2∣C2−c2A2∣​.

Use C2=a2A2−b2B2C^2=a^2A^2-b^2B^2C2=a2A2−b2B2 and c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2:

C2−c2A2=−b2(A2+B2).C^2-c^2A^2=-b^2(A^2+B^2).C2−c2A2=−b2(A2+B2).

Its absolute value gives b2b^2b2. The raw signed product is negative; lengths have a positive product.

From a curve point to the two asymptotes: write them as bx−ay=0bx-ay=0bx−ay=0 and bx+ay=0bx+ay=0bx+ay=0. The two line-normal lengths are both a2+b2\sqrt{a^2+b^2}a2+b2​:

d+d−=∣bx−ay∣ ∣bx+ay∣a2+b2=∣b2x2−a2y2∣a2+b2=a2b2a2+b2.\begin{aligned} d_+d_-&=\frac{|bx-ay|\,|bx+ay|}{a^2+b^2}\\ &=\frac{|b^2x^2-a^2y^2|}{a^2+b^2} =\boxed{\frac{a^2b^2}{a^2+b^2}}. \end{aligned}d+​d−​​=a2+b2∣bx−ay∣∣bx+ay∣​=a2+b2∣b2x2−a2y2∣​=a2+b2a2b2​​.​

The last equality uses the original hyperbola equation, multiplied by a2b2a^2b^2a2b2.

Recognition: “from the foci to a tangent” and “from a curve point to the asymptotes” name different constructions. Read the starting points and target lines before choosing either formula.

Concept C12 — Perpendicular tangents and a director-circle qualification

For an intersection point (h,k)(h,k)(h,k), a tangent slope satisfies

(k−mh)2=a2m2−b2,(k-mh)^2=a^2m^2-b^2,(k−mh)2=a2m2−b2,

so

(h2−a2)m2−2hkm+(k2+b2)=0.(h^2-a^2)m^2-2hkm+(k^2+b^2)=0.(h2−a2)m2−2hkm+(k2+b2)=0.

Perpendicular finite slopes have product −1-1−1, giving the conventional director-circle equation

h2+k2=a2−b2.\boxed{h^2+k^2=a^2-b^2}.h2+k2=a2−b2​.

When a>ba>ba>b, its radius is a2−b2\sqrt{a^2-b^2}a2−b2​.

Exact finite-contact condition: exclude the four places where this circle crosses the two asymptotes. At such a point, one algebraic slope candidate gives c0=0c_0=0c0​=0, so it is an asymptote, not a tangent touching at a finite point. Q11 preserves the conventional MCQ answer and explicitly shows these excluded points.

For a=ba=ba=b, the formal equation shrinks to the centre, but the two algebraic lines there are asymptotes. There is no pair of finite perpendicular tangents. For a<ba<ba<b, the formal radius squared is negative, so again there is no real such pair.

This is a supporting source construction. Learn the tangent/asymptote distinction first, instead of treating the director-circle formula as an unrestricted rule.

Concept C13 — Connect the locus to its exact geometric condition

For foci separated by 2c2c2c, a fixed absolute difference ddd:

  • gives a nondegenerate hyperbola when 0<d<2c0<d<2c0<d<2c;
  • gives the perpendicular bisector when d=0d=0d=0;
  • gives the two outer focal-axis rays, including the foci, when d=2cd=2cd=2c;
  • gives no point when d>2cd>2cd>2c, by the triangle inequality.

For a focus and a proper directrix line, begin with PF=e PDPF=e\,PDPF=ePD, using the perpendicular line-distance denominator. For e>1e>1e>1 this gives a hyperbola when the focus is off the line. Check the original nonnegative distances after squaring.

A right angle at the moving point gives another useful view. If PF1⊥PF2PF_1\perp PF_2PF1​⊥PF2​, then the point lies on the circle with F1F2F_1F_2F1​F2​ as diameter. A dot product means multiply matching direction components and add; it is zero for two perpendicular directions:

(P−F1)⋅(P−F2)=0.(\mathbf P-\mathbf F_1)\cdot(\mathbf P-\mathbf F_2)=0.(P−F1​)⋅(P−F2​)=0.

For foci (±c,0)(\pm c,0)(±c,0), this reduces to

x2+y2=c2.\boxed{x^2+y^2=c^2}.x2+y2=c2​.

Now combine that circle with the hyperbola, or combine the right-triangle identity with the fixed focal difference. Choose the version that directly produces the quantity asked.

Cauchy–Schwarz connection — important for JEE Main: ∣ux+vy∣≤u2+v2x2+y2|ux+vy|\le\sqrt{u^2+v^2}\sqrt{x^2+y^2}∣ux+vy∣≤u2+v2​x2+y2​ bounds a projection when the radial length is fixed, as on this circle. A hyperbola alone is unbounded, so do not copy an ellipse's finite global maximum without a new constraint. For example, xxx has no largest value on its right branch.

Last-minute formula recap

Unless stated otherwise, use the horizontal form with a,b>0a,b>0a,b>0, c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2, e=c/a>1e=c/a>1e=c/a>1. Swap coordinates for vertical opening and shift by the actual centre.

Method habit: identify the branch, line and kind of distance. A tangent has a finite contact; an asymptote is a limiting guide. Algebra must keep that geometric difference.

Worked solutions to the 25 PDF questions

Read the question first. Notice the pattern, choose a route, then calculate. Alternative methods below are fully visible.

Question 1 — Hyperbola eccentricity uses a sum of squared semiaxes

PDF page 102 | MCQ | Notes: C01,C03

The eccentricity of the hyperbola x29−y216=1\dfrac{x^2}{9}-\dfrac{y^2}{16}=19x2​−16y2​=1 is

  • (a) 54\dfrac5445​
  • (b) 43\dfrac4334​
  • (c) 53\dfrac5335​
  • (d) 259\dfrac{25}9925​

The positive term is x2/9x^2/9x2/9, so the transverse semiaxis is a=3a=3a=3. The other shape length is b=4b=4b=4. A hyperbola has c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2:

c2=9+16=25,c=5.c^2=9+16=25,\qquad c=5.c2=9+16=25,c=5.

Thus

e=ca=53;(c).\boxed{e=\frac ca=\frac53;\quad\text{(c)}}.e=ac​=35​;(c)​.

Check: a hyperbola must have e>1e>1e>1. The option 25/925/925/9 is e2e^2e2, not eee. Using an ellipse's minus sign would give a negative c2c^2c2 here.

Question 2 — Normalize before reading the latus rectum

PDF page 102 | MCQ | Notes: C02,C04

The length of the latus rectum of the hyperbola 16x2−9y2=14416x^2-9y^2=14416x2−9y2=144 is

  • (a) 323\dfrac{32}3332​
  • (b) 92\dfrac9229​
  • (c) 163\dfrac{16}3316​
  • (d) 888

Divide by 144 before reading the lengths:

x29−y216=1,a=3,b=4.\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{16}=1, \qquad a=3,\quad b=4.9x2​−16y2​=1,a=3,b=4.

The latus rectum is a full chord through a focus, perpendicular to the transverse axis:

L=2b2a=323;(a).\boxed{L=\frac{2b^2}{a}=\frac{32}3;\quad\text{(a)}}.L=a2b2​=332​;(a)​.

Coordinate check: the right focus is (5,0)(5,0)(5,0). At x=5x=5x=5, the original equation gives y=±16/3y=\pm16/3y=±16/3. Their separation is 32/332/332/3. The larger denominator belongs to b2b^2b2 here; it does not decide the transverse direction.

Question 3 — Foci and eccentricity give the transverse semiaxis

PDF page 102 | MCQ | Notes: C02,C03

The hyperbola having foci at (±5,0)(\pm5,0)(±5,0) and eccentricity 54\dfrac5445​ is

  • (a) x29−y216=1\dfrac{x^2}{9}-\dfrac{y^2}{16}=19x2​−16y2​=1
  • (b) x225−y216=1\dfrac{x^2}{25}-\dfrac{y^2}{16}=125x2​−16y2​=1
  • (c) x216+y29=1\dfrac{x^2}{16}+\dfrac{y^2}{9}=116x2​+9y2​=1
  • (d) x216−y29=1\dfrac{x^2}{16}-\dfrac{y^2}{9}=116x2​−9y2​=1

Foci give c=5c=5c=5; eccentricity gives the ratio c/ac/ac/a.

ca=54⟹a=4.\frac ca=\frac54 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=4.ac​=45​⟹a=4.

Then

b2=c2−a2=25−16=9.b^2=c^2-a^2=25-16=9.b2=c2−a2=25−16=9.

Since the foci lie on the xxx-axis,

x216−y29=1;(d).\boxed{\frac{x^2}{16}-\frac{y^2}{9}=1;\quad\text{(d)}}.16x2​−9y2​=1;(d)​.

Check: e=1+9/16=5/4e=\sqrt{1+9/16}=5/4e=1+9/16​=5/4, and c=16+9=5c=\sqrt{16+9}=5c=16+9​=5. Option (c) has a plus sign, so it is an ellipse, not the required hyperbola.

Question 4 — Compare full lengths rather than half-lengths

PDF page 102 | Numerical value | Notes: C04,C06

For a hyperbola x2a2−y2b2=1\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1a2x2​−b2y2​=1, the length of the latus rectum equals the length of the transverse axis. Then e2=e^2=e2= ____.

Both named quantities are full lengths. Latus rectum =2b2/a=2b^2/a=2b2/a and transverse axis =2a=2a=2a:

2b2a=2a⟹b2=a2.\frac{2b^2}{a}=2a \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b^2=a^2.a2b2​=2a⟹b2=a2.

With a,b>0a,b>0a,b>0, this means a=ba=ba=b.

Therefore

e2=1+b2a2=2.\boxed{e^2=1+\frac{b^2}{a^2}=2}.e2=1+a2b2​=2​.

Geometric connection: equal a,ba,ba,b give asymptote slopes ±1\pm1±1, so the asymptotes are perpendicular. This is the rectangular-hyperbola case. The requested answer is e2=2e^2=2e2=2, not e=2e=\sqrt2e=2​.

Question 5 — The conjugate swaps the two axis roles

PDF page 102 | MCQ | Notes: C06

The eccentricity of the conjugate hyperbola of x29−y216=1\dfrac{x^2}{9}-\dfrac{y^2}{16}=19x2​−16y2​=1 is

  • (a) 53\dfrac5335​
  • (b) 43\dfrac4334​
  • (c) 54\dfrac5445​
  • (d) 34\dfrac3443​

First write the conjugate, rather than reusing the original eccentricity.

y216−x29=1.\frac{y^2}{16}-\frac{x^2}{9}=1.16y2​−9x2​=1.

It opens vertically, so its transverse semiaxis is 4. Its focal distance is still 16+9=5\sqrt{16+9}=516+9​=5.

e′=54;(c).\boxed{e'=\frac54;\quad\text{(c)}}.e′=45​;(c)​.

Another quick approach: the original e=5/3e=5/3e=5/3 and 1/e2+1/e′2=11/e^2+1/e'^2=11/e2+1/e′2=1 give

1e′2=1−925=1625,\frac1{e'^2}=1-\frac9{25}=\frac{16}{25},e′21​=1−259​=2516​,

so e′=5/4e'=5/4e′=5/4. Writing the conjugate first is safer when the axis roles are not familiar.

Question 6 — Finite tangent slope and intercept must satisfy the contact condition

PDF page 102 | Numerical value | Notes: C08

If the line y=2x+cy=2x+cy=2x+c touches the hyperbola x29−y24=1\dfrac{x^2}{9}-\dfrac{y^2}{4}=19x2​−4y2​=1, then c2=c^2=c2= ____.

The line's slope is fixed at 2. For a finite tangent to x2/9−y2/4=1x^2/9-y^2/4=1x2/9−y2/4=1,

c2=a2m2−b2=9(2)2−4.c^2=a^2m^2-b^2=9(2)^2-4.c2=a2m2−b2=9(2)2−4.

Hence

c2=32.\boxed{c^2=32}.c2=32​.

The positive value means real finite contacts exist; c=±32c=\pm\sqrt{32}c=±32​ gives the two parallel tangents.

Another possible approach — repeated intersection: substituting y=2x+cy=2x+cy=2x+c gives

32x2+36cx+9c2+36=0.32x^2+36cx+9c^2+36=0.32x2+36cx+9c2+36=0.

The discriminant is 144(c2−32)144(c^2-32)144(c2−32). Setting it to zero gives the same result. The leading coefficient is 32, so no quadratic term has disappeared and the repeated root is a genuine finite contact.

Question 7 — Check a curve point before applying its tangent formula

PDF page 102 | MCQ | Notes: C08

The equation of the tangent to x29−y216=1\dfrac{x^2}{9}-\dfrac{y^2}{16}=19x2​−16y2​=1 at the point (5,163)\left(5,\dfrac{16}3\right)(5,316​) is

  • (a) 5x+3y=415x+3y=415x+3y=41
  • (b) 4x−3y=44x-3y=44x−3y=4
  • (c) 3x−5y=−13x-5y=-13x−5y=−1
  • (d) 5x−3y=95x-3y=95x−3y=9

First verify the point:

259−(16/3)216=259−169=1.\frac{25}{9}-\frac{(16/3)^2}{16} =\frac{25}{9}-\frac{16}{9}=1.925​−16(16/3)2​=925​−916​=1.

The tangent-at-point formula now applies:

5x9−(16/3)y16=1⟹5x9−y3=1.\frac{5x}{9}-\frac{(16/3)y}{16}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{5x}{9}-\frac y3=1.95x​−16(16/3)y​=1⟹95x​−3y​=1. 5x−3y=9;(d).\boxed{5x-3y=9;\quad\text{(d)}}.5x−3y=9;(d)​.

Another possible approach: differentiate x2/9−y2/16=1x^2/9-y^2/16=1x2/9−y2/16=1:

y′=16x9y.y'=\frac{16x}{9y}.y′=9y16x​.

At the point it is 5/35/35/3. Thus y−16/3=(5/3)(x−5)y-16/3=(5/3)(x-5)y−16/3=(5/3)(x−5) gives the same line.

Check: 25−16=925-16=925−16=9. The dashed auxiliary normal has slope −3/5-3/5−3/5, perpendicular to the tangent's 5/35/35/3; a normal is a different line.

Question 8 — Translate to the centre before drawing the asymptote pair

PDF page 102 | MCQ | Notes: C05

The combined equation of the asymptotes of the hyperbola 9x2−16y2−18x−32y−151=09x^2-16y^2-18x-32y-151=09x2−16y2−18x−32y−151=0 is

  • (a) 9x2−16y2−18x−32y+7=09x^2-16y^2-18x-32y+7=09x2−16y2−18x−32y+7=0
  • (b) 9x2−16y2−18x−32y−7=09x^2-16y^2-18x-32y-7=09x2−16y2−18x−32y−7=0
  • (c) 9x2−16y2−18x+32y−7=09x^2-16y^2-18x+32y-7=09x2−16y2−18x+32y−7=0
  • (d) 9x2+16y2+18x−32y−7=09x^2+16y^2+18x-32y-7=09x2+16y2+18x−32y−7=0

Find the centre before guessing the asymptotes. Complete both squares:

9[(x−1)2−1]−16[(y+1)2−1]−151=0.9[(x-1)^2-1]-16[(y+1)^2-1]-151=0.9[(x−1)2−1]−16[(y+1)2−1]−151=0.

Thus

9(x−1)2−16(y+1)2=144.9(x-1)^2-16(y+1)^2=144.9(x−1)2−16(y+1)2=144.

The centre is (1,−1)(1,-1)(1,−1). The asymptote pair uses the same squared terms with zero on the right:

9(x−1)2−16(y+1)2=0.9(x-1)^2-16(y+1)^2=0.9(x−1)2−16(y+1)2=0.

Expand:

9x2−16y2−18x−32y−7=0;(b).\boxed{9x^2-16y^2-18x-32y-7=0;\quad\text{(b)}}.9x2−16y2−18x−32y−7=0;(b)​.

Another possible approach: factor first:

[3(x−1)−4(y+1)][3(x−1)+4(y+1)]=0.[3(x-1)-4(y+1)][3(x-1)+4(y+1)]=0.[3(x−1)−4(y+1)][3(x−1)+4(y+1)]=0.

The two lines are 3x−4y−7=03x-4y-7=03x−4y−7=0 and 3x+4y+1=03x+4y+1=03x+4y+1=0. Multiplying gives the selected pair.

Check: both lines pass through (1,−1)(1,-1)(1,−1). Changing only the constant in the original equation without locating the centre risks the wrong sign.

Question 9 — Distinguish the acute angle from its supplementary angle

PDF page 102 | Numerical value | Notes: C03,C05

The eccentricity of a hyperbola is 222. The acute angle (in degrees) between its asymptotes is ____.

Eccentricity tells the asymptote slope ratio:

e2=1+b2a2=4⟹ba=3.e^2=1+\frac{b^2}{a^2}=4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac ba=\sqrt3.e2=1+a2b2​=4⟹ab​=3​.

So the asymptotes have slopes ±3\pm\sqrt3±3​. They make angles 60∘60^\circ60∘ and 120∘120^\circ120∘ with the positive xxx-axis.

The smaller angle between those directions is

120∘−60∘=60∘.\boxed{120^\circ-60^\circ=60^\circ}.120∘−60∘=60∘​.

Another possible approach: the acute angle θ\thetaθ satisfies

tan⁡θ=∣231−3∣=3.\tan\theta=\left|\frac{2\sqrt3}{1-3}\right|=\sqrt3.tanθ=​1−323​​​=3​.

Since the question says acute, select θ=60∘\theta=60^\circθ=60∘, not its supplement 120∘120^\circ120∘. The drawing helps choose the sector; the slope calculation fixes its exact size.

Question 10 — A fixed absolute difference of focal distances gives both branches

PDF page 103 | MCQ | Notes: C01,C13

The locus of a point PPP such that ∣PF1−PF2∣=6|PF_1-PF_2|=6∣PF1​−PF2​∣=6, where F1=(5,0)F_1=(5,0)F1​=(5,0), F2=(−5,0)F_2=(-5,0)F2​=(−5,0), is

  • (a) x29−y216=1\dfrac{x^2}{9}-\dfrac{y^2}{16}=19x2​−16y2​=1
  • (b) x216−y29=1\dfrac{x^2}{16}-\dfrac{y^2}{9}=116x2​−9y2​=1
  • (c) x29+y216=1\dfrac{x^2}{9}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=19x2​+16y2​=1
  • (d) x236−y225=1\dfrac{x^2}{36}-\dfrac{y^2}{25}=136x2​−25y2​=1

An absolute focal-distance difference is the hyperbola definition.

2a=6⟹a=3.2a=6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=3.2a=6⟹a=3.

The foci are (±5,0)(\pm5,0)(±5,0), so c=5c=5c=5. Therefore

b2=c2−a2=25−9=16.b^2=c^2-a^2=25-9=16.b2=c2−a2=25−9=16. x29−y216=1;(a).\boxed{\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{16}=1;\quad\text{(a)}}.9x2​−16y2​=1;(a)​.

Check the definition at both vertices: at (3,0)(3,0)(3,0) the distances are 2 and 8; at (−3,0)(-3,0)(−3,0) they are 8 and 2. In both cases their absolute difference is 6. The focal separation is 10, greater than the requested difference, so the nondegenerate locus is possible.

Question 11 — Perpendicular tangents give a director circle with finite-contact exclusions

PDF page 103 | MCQ | Notes: C12

The locus of the point of intersection of perpendicular tangents to x216−y29=1\dfrac{x^2}{16}-\dfrac{y^2}{9}=116x2​−9y2​=1 is

  • (a) x2+y2=25x^2+y^2=25x2+y2=25
  • (b) x2+y2=12x^2+y^2=12x2+y2=12
  • (c) x2+y2=9x^2+y^2=9x2+y2=9
  • (d) x2+y2=7x^2+y^2=7x2+y2=7

Start with the usual director-circle result, then check what “tangent” means here. For the hyperbola, a2=16,b2=9a^2=16,b^2=9a2=16,b2=9. The conventional equation for perpendicular tangent intersections is

x2+y2=16−9=7;intended (d).\boxed{x^2+y^2=16-9=7;\quad\text{intended (d)}}.x2+y2=16−9=7;intended (d)​.

Why this equation appears: a tangent through (h,k)(h,k)(h,k) gives

(h2−16)m2−2hkm+(k2+9)=0.(h^2-16)m^2-2hkm+(k^2+9)=0.(h2−16)m2−2hkm+(k2+9)=0.

For perpendicular finite slopes, their product is −1-1−1:

k2+9h2−16=−1⟹h2+k2=7.\frac{k^2+9}{h^2-16}=-1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad h^2+k^2=7.h2−16k2+9​=−1⟹h2+k2=7.

Check a genuine pair: at P=(0,7)P=(0,\sqrt7)P=(0,7​), the lines y=x+7y=x+\sqrt7y=x+7​ and y=−x+7y=-x+\sqrt7y=−x+7​ have slopes 1,−11,-11,−1 and satisfy the finite tangent condition 7=16−9>07=16-9>07=16−9>0.

Exact finite-contact qualification: remove the four points where this circle crosses the asymptotes y=±3x/4y=\pm3x/4y=±3x/4:

(±475, ±375),\left(\pm\frac{4\sqrt7}{5},\ \pm\frac{3\sqrt7}{5}\right),(±547​​, ±537​​),

with independent sign choices. At one of these points, one slope candidate gives an intercept zero. That line is an asymptote and never touches the hyperbola at a finite point. The source uses the conventional circle equation; the exact locus of intersections of two finite-contact perpendicular tangents is this circle without those four points.

This exception is why we keep the strict condition c02=16m2−9>0c_0^2=16m^2-9>0c02​=16m2−9>0, rather than counting every algebraic candidate as a tangent.

PDF page 103 | MCQ | Notes: C04

The point (8,33)(8,3\sqrt3)(8,33​) lies on x216−y29=1\dfrac{x^2}{16}-\dfrac{y^2}{9}=116x2​−9y2​=1. Its distance from the focus (5,0)(5,0)(5,0) is

Question 15 — The transverse axis of xy8 is rotated

PDF page 103 | Numerical value | Notes: C07

The length of the transverse axis of the rectangular hyperbola xy=8xy=8xy=8 is ____.

The coordinate axes are the asymptotes of xy=8xy=8xy=8. The transverse axis is a diagonal. We cannot read 8 as a squared horizontal semiaxis.

Use perpendicular diagonal coordinates

u=x+y2,v=x−y2.u=\frac{x+y}{\sqrt2},\qquad v=\frac{x-y}{\sqrt2}.u=2​x+y​,v=2​x−y​.

Since u2−v2=2xy=16u^2-v^2=2xy=16u2−v2=2xy=16,

u216−v216=1.\frac{u^2}{16}-\frac{v^2}{16}=1.16u2​−16v2​=1.

Thus its transverse semiaxis is 4 and

2a=8.\boxed{2a=8}.2a=8​.

Another geometric approach — locate the nearest points to the centre: along the positive branch,

x2+y2≥2xy=16,x^2+y^2\ge2xy=16,x2+y2≥2xy=16,

with equality at x=y=8x=y=\sqrt8x=y=8​. The opposite vertex is (−8,−8)(-\sqrt8,-\sqrt8)(−8​,−8​). Each is 4 units from the origin, so the full transverse length is 8. This AM–GM view is shorter if a rotation formula is unfamiliar.

Check: both vertices have product 8 and their direct separation is (28)2+(28)2=8\sqrt{(2\sqrt8)^2+(2\sqrt8)^2}=8(28​)2+(28​)2​=8.
